Mapping Telehealth Deserts

When the clinic is an hour away and the Wi-Fi won't hold a video call, there is no virtual care either.

We joined HRSA's Medically Underserved Areas with FCC broadband tier data and found 207 counties where both access gaps compound. This is the story the public doesn't yet know we can tell.

Chapter 01

Your healthcare work is already making a difference

HRSA's Medically Underserved Area program has done something difficult: it has made invisible need visible. Across 2,775 counties, your agency has documented exactly where the healthcare system falls short, and has been pivotal in shrinking the healthcare gap for all Americans.

But clinics are no longer just a buildings. Telehealth, now a permanent solution for millions, means care also arrives through a broadband connection. Virtual visits, remote monitoring, digital prescriptions. The question is no longer only where is the nearest doctor? It is also: can the patient get online to see one?

The MUA designation identifies where physical care is absent. It was not designed to capture whether a patient can access virtual care instead. That gap, between what the data shows and what residents actually experience, is our opportunity to make an impact.
Chapter 02

Broadband has gotten better — but not everywhere that matters

The federal government's response was the Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) program. Through BEAD $42.5 billion were planned to close the connectivity gap once and for all.

But funding alone does not guarantee the right outcomes. Without a health-centered lens on allocation, dollars will flow to states and counties based on connectivity metrics alone, without visibility into where broadband absence most directly translates into a failure to access care.

How Speed Works
Who is left behind
FCC Form 477 uses a tier scale to measure broadband speeds, as well as the number of connections per 1,000 households in each county.
Connections / 1,000 households by speed threshold
A county with a Tier 3 score ≤ 2 means 400 or fewer connections per 1,000 households at 25 Mbps. This is the FCC threshold for "unserved" — and the minimum speed needed for a single reliable telehealth visit.

Chapter 03

There is an actionable opportunity at the intersection nobody has mapped — Telehealth Deserts

By joining HRSA's MUA designations with FCC Form 477 county-level broadband tier data on FIPS codes, we identified a specific, bounded population: counties where residents cannot reliably reach an in-person doctor and where fewer than 40% of households have a fixed 25 Mbps connection. These 207 telehealth desert counties are not arbitrary. They are places your agency has already documented as having documented healthcare shortages. Compounded by the broadband gap, the populations that already lack physical access to healthcare now risk being virtually underserved as well.

Healthcare gap — too broad. Telehealth deserts — actionable. For the first time, we have the opportunity to move beyond a list of 2,775 counties and act with precision: 207 places where closing the broadband gap is not just an infrastructure decision, but also a healthcare intervention.

Chapter 04

A deeper look: the burden doesn't stop at broadband

The 207 telehealth desert counties are not just connectivity failures. They are already some of the most vulnerable populations in the country. They carry higher rates of chronic disease, deeper poverty, and fewer safety nets than the rest of the nation. Broadband absence does not create their vulnerability. It compounds it.

⊕ Opportunity — Indigenous Communities

Tribal land overlaps with telehealth desert counties. A disproportionate share of unserved broadband zones fall within or adjacent to federally recognized tribal areas.

⊕ Opportunity — Infant Mortality

Infant mortality rates in desert counties exceed national averages. Telehealth prenatal care has demonstrated measurable impact — these counties are not receiving it.

⊕ Opportunity — Food Deserts

USDA food desert designations overlap significantly with telehealth desert counties — compounding nutrition-related chronic disease burden in the same populations.

Not all 207 counties are equal. To prioritize the most vulnerable, we built a Composite Telehealth Crisis Index (CTCI) — a weighted score that identifies where all four crises converge at their most acute, so the first dollar goes to the highest-need county.

We built a Composite Telehealth Crisis Index (CTCI) that weighs four dimensions simultaneously:

  • 35% — Healthcare access gap: how far below the MUA threshold each county's IMU score falls
  • 30% — Broadband gap: FCC Tier 3 connectivity deficit (25/3 Mbps household coverage)
  • 20% — Chronic disease burden: adult obesity prevalence from CDC PLACES 2024
  • 15% — Economic vulnerability: county poverty rate from ACS 5-Year 2023 B17001 (all counties covered)

The table below scores U.S. telehealth desert counties on this index. The top 10 counties are where all Americans are the most vulnerable. These are not abstract statistics. They are the specific places where the first BEAD health-targeting dollars will have the highest return.

Addressing these gaps is not just a connectivity challenge, but also a health equity imperative. The CTCI gives us a tool to ensure that BEAD funding reaches the people who need it most: communities where every dollar of broadband investment translates directly into access to care.

Chapter 05

The ask

There are 207 Telehealth Deserts. 207 counties where people risk being left behind. 207 counties where we have a chance to make a tangible impact.

The Brief · For the CMO

This is a communications asset, not just a map. Today you are seeing 20% of what it could be.

Pair HRSA's mission with a story the public and press can hold in their hands. A composite severity index, county drill-down, and shareable embed would turn 207 counties into a narrative states, media, and legislators can act on — during the one BEAD allocation window we get.

Our ask
  • 6 weeks of analyst time — a team of 4 — to build the composite severity index, county drill-down, and expanded comorbidity layers.
  • Publicly available data only — HRSA, FCC, CDC, ACS. No licensing costs, no additional data acquisition.
  • Lightweight infrastructure — static files, no database, no cloud storage costs. Fully portable and embeddable.

Chapter 06

What's next — a roadmap for deeper impact

What you have seen today is the surface. Our analysis was intentionally scoped to the most conservative definition of broadband absence — fully unserved counties at 25 Mbps. 3.5 million Americans is already a large number, worthy of immediate action. But expand that lens to underserved communities, and the 3.5 million people in 207 becomes a much larger, more urgent number.

01 · Scratching the Surface

We only looked at fully unserved broadband (below 25 Mbps). Underserved communities — those with technically available but unreliable connectivity — represent an even larger population at risk. Expanding the threshold tells a bigger, more complete story.

02 · Communities Left Behind

Indigenous communities, historically redlined neighborhoods, and persistent poverty counties show systematic overlap with telehealth deserts. An equity-centered analysis would map these structural histories onto the broadband gap — making the case for targeted, community-led investment.

03 · The Ultimate Goal

Build a living resource that helps states take a human approach to allocating BEAD funding — one that centers health outcomes, not just connectivity metrics. A shareable, embeddable tool that HRSA, state BEAD offices, and legislators can use during the one allocation window we have.
